title: Inverse Trigonometric Functions
learningObjective: Determine the inverse sine, cosine, and tangent values; graph inverse trigonometric functions and determine the limitations on the domain and range.

faqs.question: Why do we need inverse trig functions, and why can't we just invert sine, cosine, and tangent directly?
faqs.answer: Inverting a function requires it to be one-to-one (FN6) — but sine, cosine, and tangent are each far from one-to-one over their full domain, since infinitely many angles share the exact same sine, cosine, or tangent value. For example, \( \cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) \) and \( \cos\left(\dfrac{5\pi}{3}\right) \) are both \( \dfrac{1}{2} \) — so "the angle whose cosine is 1/2" can't have one honest answer unless we agree to restrict which angles we're allowed to pick from.

faqs.question: What is arcsine, and what domain restriction defines it?
faqs.answer:
Arcsine, written \( \arcsin(x) \), is the inverse of sine restricted to the domain \( \left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2},\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right] \) — the one continuous stretch of the sine curve that's actually one-to-one, hitting every output exactly once. \( \arcsin(x) \) is the unique angle \( \theta \) in that restricted interval such that \( \sin(\theta)=x \).

Only the highlighted middle piece of sine — where it's one-to-one — gets used to define arcsine.

faqs.question: What is arccosine, and what domain restriction defines it?
faqs.answer: Arccosine, written \( \arccos(x) \), is the inverse of cosine restricted to the domain \( [0,\pi] \) — the interval where cosine steadily decreases from 1 down to −1 without ever repeating a value. \( \arccos(x) \) is the unique angle \( \theta \) in that restricted interval such that \( \cos(\theta)=x \).

faqs.question: What is arctangent, and why is its domain restriction an open interval instead of closed?
faqs.answer: Arctangent, written \( \arctan(x) \), is the inverse of tangent restricted to \( \left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2},\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) \) — using PARENTHESES rather than brackets, because tangent itself is undefined at \( \pm\dfrac{\pi}{2} \) (PF2's vertical asymptotes). Since those endpoints were never part of tangent's domain to begin with, they can't be included in arctangent's restriction either.

faqs.question: Why doesn't sin⁻¹(x) mean the same thing as (sin(x))⁻¹?
faqs.answer: This notation is genuinely ambiguous at first glance, and it's worth being deliberate about it. \( \sin^{-1}(x) \) is just shorthand — commonly used on calculators — for \( \arcsin(x) \), the inverse FUNCTION. It does NOT mean "raise sin(x) to the power −1," which would actually be \( \dfrac{1}{\sin(x)}=\csc(x) \) instead. Whenever there's doubt, writing \( \arcsin(x) \) instead of \( \sin^{-1}(x) \) avoids the confusion entirely.

faqs.question: How do I evaluate an inverse trig function like arcsin or arccos at a special angle value, without a calculator?
faqs.answer:
Ask yourself: "what angle, within the correct restricted interval, has this value as its sine (or cosine, or tangent)?" Use your TR4/TR5 special-angle knowledge to recall which angle produces that value, then double check it actually falls within the required restricted range.
Worked Example

\( \arcsin\left(-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) \): which angle in \( \left[-\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{\pi}{2}\right] \) has sine \( -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \)?

\( \arcsin\left(-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) = -\dfrac{\pi}{3} \)

faqs.question: How do I evaluate an inverse trig function using a calculator?
faqs.answer:
Use the \( \sin^{-1} \), \( \cos^{-1} \), or \( \tan^{-1} \) button (usually accessed via a SHIFT or 2nd function key above the regular sin/cos/tan buttons). Make sure your calculator's angle mode (degrees or radians) matches what the problem is asking for before you evaluate.
Worked Example

\( \arccos\left(-\dfrac{3}{5}\right) \approx 126.9° \) or \( \approx 2.21 \) radians

faqs.question: What is the domain and range of arcsine, arccosine, and arctangent?
faqs.answer:
Each function's domain matches the restricted-input function's range, and each range matches the restricted domain that was chosen.
Summary

\( \arcsin(x) \): domain \( [-1,1] \), range \( \left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2},\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right] \)

\( \arccos(x) \): domain \( [-1,1] \), range \( [0,\pi] \)

\( \arctan(x) \): domain \( (-\infty,\infty) \), range \( \left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2},\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) \)

faqs.question: How do I graph arcsine, arccosine, or arctangent?
faqs.answer:
Each inverse trig graph is the mirror image, across the line \( y=x \), of the restricted piece of its original trig function (the exact same idea from EL4's log/exponential mirror-image relationship) — so the fastest way to sketch it is to take a few known points from the restricted original function and swap the x- and y-coordinates.

arcsin(x): a compact S-curve, defined only on [−1, 1], with range [−π/2, π/2].

faqs.question: How do I evaluate a composition like sin(arccos(5/13)) exactly, without a calculator?
faqs.answer:
Let \( \theta=\arccos\left(\dfrac{5}{13}\right) \), draw a right triangle with angle \( \theta \) where the adjacent side is 5 and the hypotenuse is 13, use the Pythagorean theorem to find the missing side, then read off whichever trig ratio the outer function is asking for.

Adjacent = 5, hypotenuse = 13, so the missing side (opposite) = 12 — giving sin(θ) = 12/13.

Worked Example

Missing side: \( \sqrt{13^2-5^2}=\sqrt{144}=12 \)

\( \sin\left(\arccos\left(\dfrac{5}{13}\right)\right)=\sin(\theta)=\dfrac{12}{13} \)

faqs.question: How do I know which right triangle to draw when evaluating a composition of a trig function and an inverse trig function?
faqs.answer: Look at what's INSIDE the inverse trig function — that fraction directly tells you two of the triangle's three sides. If it's \( \arcsin\left(\dfrac{a}{b}\right) \), the opposite side is \( a \) and the hypotenuse is \( b \) (since sine is opposite/hypotenuse). If it's \( \arccos\left(\dfrac{a}{b}\right) \), the adjacent side is \( a \) and the hypotenuse is \( b \). If it's \( \arctan\left(\dfrac{a}{b}\right) \), the opposite side is \( a \) and the adjacent side is \( b \). Whichever two sides you're given, the Pythagorean theorem finds the third.

faqs.question: How do I evaluate a composition like cos(arcsin(x)) that has a variable instead of a number?
faqs.answer:
Use the exact same triangle method from faq-10 and faq-11 — just with \( x \) standing in for one of the sides instead of a specific number.
Worked Example

Find \( \cos(\arcsin(x)) \). Since \( \arcsin(x) \) means opposite \( =x \), hypotenuse \( =1 \):

Missing side (adjacent): \( \sqrt{1-x^2} \)

\( \cos(\arcsin(x)) = \dfrac{\text{adjacent}}{\text{hypotenuse}} = \sqrt{1-x^2} \)

faqs.question: How does this section connect to FN6's inverse function ideas and TR5's exact trig values?
faqs.answer: This section is FN6's entire inverse-function framework — one-to-one requirement, domain restriction, domain/range swapping — applied specifically to sine, cosine, and tangent. And every "evaluate without a calculator" question here leans directly on TR5's reference-angle and exact-value work, just run in the opposite direction: instead of angle → trig value, you're going trig value → angle.

faqs.question: Why do inverse trig functions matter beyond this course?
faqs.answer: Any time you know a ratio (a slope, a height-to-distance ratio, a physical measurement) and need to find the actual ANGLE that produced it — like the carpenter's ramp problem, navigation, physics, or engineering — you need an inverse trig function. They're also essential in calculus, where derivatives and integrals involving inverse trig functions show up constantly once you start working with more advanced techniques.
